terms.definition: A digital storage system that stores data so it can be saved, retrieved, updated, and deleted efficiently.
terms.example: Think of it like a digital filing cabinet that stores all your college records.

terms.definition: Database Management System — software that creates, manages, secures, and optimizes a database.
terms.example: MySQL is a DBMS. It is like the librarian who manages your library (the database).

terms.definition: Structured Query Language — the language used to communicate with relational databases.
terms.example: Writing SELECT * FROM students; retrieves all student records instantly.

terms.definition: Data organized in a fixed, predefined format — typically rows and columns in a table.
terms.example: A student table with id, name, age, and department columns is structured data.

terms.definition: Data that does not use a fixed table format but still has some internal structure using tags or key-value pairs.
terms.example: A JSON file like {name: 'Amit', age: 20} is semi-structured.

terms.definition: Data with no predefined format or organization — cannot fit neatly into rows and columns.
terms.example: Images, videos, audio files, and raw PDFs are unstructured data.

terms.definition: Relational Database Management System — a DBMS that organizes data into related tables using SQL.
terms.example: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server are all RDBMS software.

terms.definition: A category of databases designed for semi-structured or unstructured data with flexible schemas.
terms.example: MongoDB (document), Redis (key-value), Cassandra (column) are NoSQL databases.

terms.definition: Data Definition Language — SQL commands used to define or modify the structure of tables and databases.
terms.example: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, and TRUNCATE are DDL commands.

terms.definition: Data Manipulation Language — SQL commands used to add, modify, or delete data inside tables.
terms.example: INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE are DML commands.

terms.definition: Data Query Language — SQL commands used to retrieve or fetch data from tables.
terms.example: SELECT is the only DQL command and is the most frequently used SQL command.

terms.definition: Data Control Language — SQL commands that manage user permissions on databases and tables.
terms.example: GRANT gives permissions; REVOKE removes them.

terms.definition: Transaction Control Language — SQL commands that manage safe, atomic transactions involving multiple DML operations.
terms.example: COMMIT saves changes permanently; ROLLBACK undoes them; SAVEPOINT creates a checkpoint.

terms.definition: A column (or group of columns) that uniquely identifies each record in a table. Must be unique and not NULL.
terms.example: The student id column set as PRIMARY KEY ensures no two students share the same ID.

terms.definition: A variable-length text data type in SQL. The number in brackets sets the maximum character limit.
terms.example: name VARCHAR(50) stores names up to 50 characters long.

terms.definition: A SQL join that returns only the rows where both tables have a matching value based on the ON condition.
terms.example: INNER JOIN between students and departments returns only students whose department exists in the departments table.

terms.definition: A SQL join that returns all rows from the left table and matching rows from the right table. Unmatched rows show NULL.
terms.example: LEFT JOIN keeps all students, even if their department has no entry in the departments table.

terms.definition: A SQL clause that groups rows sharing the same value in a specified column, allowing aggregate functions per group.
terms.example: GROUP BY department gives one row per department, and COUNT(*) shows how many students are in each.

terms.definition: A SQL clause that filters grouped results AFTER GROUP BY is applied. Used with aggregate functions.
terms.example: HAVING COUNT(*) > 10 shows only departments that have more than 10 students.

terms.definition: A DBMS feature that allows multiple users to access and modify data simultaneously without conflict or corruption.
terms.example: Hundreds of teachers and admins can update student records at the same time — DBMS manages conflicts automatically.

terms.definition: A MySQL configuration setting that controls which network interface the MySQL server listens on for incoming connections.
terms.example: Setting bind-address = 0.0.0.0 allows MySQL to accept connections from any network interface.

terms.definition: The default TCP port that MySQL uses for all incoming database connections.
terms.example: When connecting remotely with mysql -h <ip> -u user -p, the connection goes through port 3306 by default.

terms.definition: A DDL command that removes all rows from a table extremely fast without logging individual deletions. Table structure is kept.
terms.example: TRUNCATE students; removes all student rows instantly — faster than DELETE FROM students;

terms.definition: A SQL keyword that removes duplicate values from the result set, returning only unique entries.
terms.example: SELECT DISTINCT department FROM students; returns each department name only once, even if many students share it.
